approachQuestion.prompt: Checking one-way connections. You are given a directed graph as adjacency lists, a starting point s, and a destination t. Return true exactly when a directed path from s to t exists. You do not need to find the shortest path. Example: s:[a,b], a:[c], b:[], c:[t], t:[] returns true for destination t and false for destination b when starting at c. Choose a method that handles cycles and does not assume that edges work in both directions.
constraints: The directed graph may contain cycles and unreachable vertices.
The adjacency lists are ready; each directed edge appears only in the list of its source.
Each vertex has a unique identifier; s and t are vertices in the graph; 1 <= V <= 1,000,000.
You do not need to reconstruct a path or minimize its length.
Visited-set lookups and queue or stack operations take expected constant time.
This is a Premium problem; its required family is graph_traversal.

options.text: Run iterative depth-first search from s using a stack. Mark each vertex when pushing it, and stop when t is discovered.
options.feedback: This explores vertices reachable from s, and the visited set prevents cycles from causing repeated work.

options.text: Run recursive depth-first search without recording visited vertices.
options.feedback: A cycle can repeat forever. For s:[a], a:[s,t], the traversal can revisit s and a indefinitely instead of guaranteeing an answer.

options.text: Treat every edge as bidirectional, then search from s.
options.feedback: Ignoring direction can report a route that does not exist. For s:[], a:[s], start=s, destination=a, the only edge points from a to s, so the answer is false.

options.text: Run breadth-first search from s with a visited set and check whether t is discovered.
options.feedback: This also visits the vertices reachable from s. Layer order is unnecessary for a yes-or-no reachability result, but using a queue is still correct.

feedback.reason: Reachability must respect edge direction and avoid revisiting vertices in cycles. Either depth-first or breadth-first traversal can answer yes or no.

complexityQuestion.prompt: Choose the time and additional-space pair for iterative-dfs-reachability. V is the number of vertices and E is the number of directed edges. Exclude the input adjacency lists and the boolean result. Include the visited set and explicit stack; visited lookups take expected constant time. Consider the worst case, when the destination is unreachable or found last.
constraints: Each reachable vertex is pushed onto the stack at most once because it is marked when pushed.
The iterative stack does not use a recursive call stack.

options.text: O(V + E) time, O(V) additional space
O(E log E + V) time, O(E + V) additional space

feedback.reason: Each reachable vertex is removed from the stack once, and its outgoing adjacency list is scanned once. Together, those lists contain at most E edges. The stack and visited set each hold at most one entry per reachable vertex.

methodReveal.title: Iterative depth-first reachability with a visited set
methodReveal.description: Put the start vertex on a stack and mark it visited immediately. Repeat: remove a vertex; if it is the destination, return true. For each outgoing edge to an unvisited vertex, mark that vertex when pushing it onto the stack. Do not add reverse edges. If the stack becomes empty, return false.
